L130: ### 2.2 Topologically tame actions
L131: 
L132: Let G be a group, X be a surface and \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) be an injective homomorphism. We say that the action of \(\theta (G)\) is tame on X if there is a Galois locally finite branched cover \(Q:X \rightarrow Y\) with deck group \(\theta (G)\) (in particular, G is countable).
L133: ### 2.3 Belyi pairs and dessins
L134: Let \(S^{2}\) be the standard 2-dimensional sphere and fix three different points \(p_{0}, p_{1}, p_{\infty } \in S^{2}\).

Finally note that the configuration used to replace edges is rigid, meaning it has no non-trivial automorphisms. L165: ### Lemma 1
L166: 
L167: Let \(\mathcal {G}\) be a cubic connected graph with properly 3-labeled edges. Then, every \(G\le \mathrm{Aut}_{LGraph}(\mathcal {G})\) acts freely on the vertices of \(\mathcal {G}\).
L168: ### Proof
L169: Take \(G\le \mathrm{Aut}_{LGraph}{\mathcal {G}}\) and \(g\in G\). Suppose \(g(v)=v\) for some vertex v of \(\mathcal {G}\). For every other vertex w, consider a path from v to w. Since g is an automorphism of labeled graphs it must preserve the labelling of the path \(v\rightarrow w\). Suppose this path is \(v=v_0, v_1,\dots v_n=w\), and suppose the edges of \(\mathcal {G}\) are labeled with \(\left\{ 1,2,3\right\} \).
L170: We know that the edge between \(g(v_0)\) and \(g(v_1)\) has the same label as the edge between \(v_0\) and \(v_1\). However, \(g(v_0)=v_0\) and at any vertex of \(\mathcal {G}\), there is only one adjacent edge for each label. This means the edge is the same and thus, \(g(v_1)=v_1\). Clearly, by finite induction we arrive at \(g(w)=w\). And since w was arbitrary, \(g=id\). Hence, G acts freely on \(\mathcal {G}\). \(\square \)
L171: ### 2.5 Certain hyperbolic right-angle hexagons
L172: 
L173: Our proof of Theorem 【42†2】 is built upon the existence of hyperbolic pants, that is hyperbolic hexagons, whose side lenghts are different enough. The next result shows these hexagons do exist.
L174: 
L175: ### Lemma 2
L176: 
L177: There exists a hyperbolic right-angled hexagon with edges of length \(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,a_3,b_3\), such that all lengths are different and \(a_i<1<b_i\) for \(i=1,2,3\).
L178: ### Proof
L179: 
L180: For any \(l,\epsilon >0\), there exists a hyperbolic right-angled hexagon such that three non-consecutive edges have lengths \(l,l+\epsilon \) and \(l-\epsilon \) [【43†13】]. Let \(\alpha \), \(\beta \), and \(\gamma \) be the lengths of the edges opposing the edges of length l, \(l+\epsilon \), and \(l-\epsilon \) respectively. It is known that [【44†14】],
L181: $$\begin{aligned} \alpha =\cosh ^{-1}\left( \frac{\cosh (l+\epsilon )\cosh (l-\epsilon )+\cosh (l)}{\sinh (l+\epsilon )\sinh (l-\epsilon )}\right) . \end{aligned}$$
L182: 
L183: By taking limits when \(l\rightarrow \infty \) and \(\epsilon \rightarrow 0\), \(\alpha \) goes to 0, and this is also true for \(\beta \) and \(\gamma \). Therefore, by taking l big enough and \(\epsilon \) small enough we can have \(0<\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma<1<l-\epsilon<l<l+\epsilon \). Finally, it can be also shown that [【44†14】],
L184: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\sinh l}{\sinh \alpha }=\frac{\sinh (l+\epsilon )}{\sinh \beta }=\frac{\sinh (l-\epsilon )}{\sinh \gamma }. \end{aligned}$$
L185: 
L186: And since \(\sinh \) is a strictly increasing function, we deduce that \(\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma \) are all different. \(\square \)
L187: ## 3 Proof of Theorem 【45†1】
L188: ### Proof
L189: 
L190: The result is already known for the trivial group [【35†10】, 【36†11】] so we may assume G is not trivial.
L191: 
L192: Choose \(a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3\) as in Lemma 【46†2】. Denote as P the pair of hyperbolic pants obtained from glueing two copies of the hexagon given by the lemma along the edges of length \(b_1,b_2,b_3\). The surface P has three closed geodesics of length \(2a_1,2a_2,2a_3\) as boundary. We will label them with 1, 2, 3 respectively.
L193: 
L194: 【47†Image: figure c†media.springernature.com】
L195: Now, we build X as follows. Consider \(\mathcal {G}\) the graph associated to G given by Theorem 【48†3】. For each vertex v of \(\mathcal {G}\), consider an isometric copy \(P_v\) of P. And, for every edge labeled \(i\in \left\{ 1,2,3\right\} \) between vertices v and w, glue the pants \(P_v\) and \(P_w\) by isometrically identifying the geodesics with said label (thus without creating any twists).
L196: Since the set of vertices of \(\mathcal {G}\) is countable, we get an hyperbolic orientable surface X. If G is finite, the set of vertices of \(\mathcal {G}\) is also finite, so X would be closed. Also note that G permutes vertices in \(\mathcal {G}\), that is it permutes pants, thus \(\mathrm{Isom}^{+}(X)\cong G\). Indeed, an isometry maps closed geodesics into closed geodesics.
L197: The closed geodesics in X are those from the boundary of each pair of pants, of lengths \(2a_1,2a_2,2a_3<2\), and those that appear after joining at least three pants together, these ones have at least three geodesic segments of length \(b_i>1\), so their length is at least 3. Thus, the isometry must send the boundary of each pair of pants into another boundary. Therefore, isometries map pants into pants, allowing to translate them as automorphisms of \(\mathcal {G}\).
L198: Also, the geodesics from the boundaries map to a geodesic of the same length, thus, it preserves the labelling of edges in \(\mathcal {G}\). This proves i).
L199: Let us now build the dessin \(\mathcal {D}_G\). For each vertex v of \(\mathcal {G}\), consider the following graph on \(P_v\):
L200: 
L201: 【49†Image: figure d†media.springernature.com】
L202: On the 3 edges connecting two black vertices we place an alternating sequence of white-black vertices so that the resulting graph is bipartite. Each of these sequences has different length and all of them have length greater than the cycles on the boundary of P. Note that the surface obtained by removing this graph from \(P_v\) is homeomorphic to the disjoint union of two open disks.
L203: By repeating the same pattern on all the pants, we obtain a graph \(\mathcal {D}_G\) which makes \((X,\mathcal {D}_G)\) a dessin.
L204: Finally, given a subgroup \(H\le G\) we define \(\mathcal {D}_H\) as follows: Fix some \(v_0\in \mathcal {G}\) and remove from \(\mathcal {D}_G\) the vertices from the G-orbit of \(v_0\) that are not in its H-orbit. This gives \(\mathcal {D}_H\le \mathcal {D}_G\) which makes \((X,\mathcal {D}_H)\) a dessin. And it is clear that this definition satisfies iii).
L205: Take an automorphism \(f\in \mathrm{Aut}(X,\mathcal {D}_H)\). On each pair of pants \(P_v\), f preserves cycles on the boundary and thus, also the geodesics, so it must be induced by an element of \(\mathrm{Isom}^{+}(X)\). This shows \(\mathrm{Aut}(X,\mathcal {D}_H)=\left\{ h\in \mathrm{Isom}^{+}(X)\ |\ h(\mathcal {D}_H)=\mathcal {D}_H\right\} \). Thus, \(f\equiv h|_{\mathcal {D}_H}\) with \(h\in \mathrm{Isom}^{+}(X)\) and \(h(\mathcal {D}_H)=\mathcal {D}_H\).

L47: ## Abstract
L48: 
L49: It is known that every finite group can be represented as the full group of automorphisms of a suitable compact dessin d’enfant. In this paper, we give a constructive and easy proof that the same holds for any countable group by considering non-compact dessins. Moreover, we show that any tame action of a countable group is so realisable.

L69: ## 1 Introduction
L70: 
L71: In this paper, all surfaces are assumed to be orientable, connected, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. If X is a surface, then we denote by \(\mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) the group of its orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms. A topological action (or just an action) of an abstract group G on a surface X is an injective homomorphism \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) such that \(\theta (G)\) acts tame on X (see Sect. 【26†2】).
L72: Every surface admits a Riemann surface structure and, if S is a Riemann surface different from the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, the punctured plane, a torus, an annulus, the hyperbolic plane or the punctured hyperbolic plane, then its group \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\) of conformal automorphisms is a countable group.
L73: Conversely, in [【27†8】], Greenberg proved that for every countable (finite or infinite) group G there is a Riemann surface S (which can be assumed to be compact if G is finite) and an injective homomorphism \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(S)\). Moreover, \(\theta \) may be assumed to be an isomorphism (by using maximal Fuchsian groups). A short proof of the previous fact has been given by Allcock in [【28†1】] (see also [【29†15】]).
L104: In particular, the strong symmetric genus of a finite group is also the minimal genus action at the level of Grothendieck’s dessins. The proof of such result was done in terms of Riemann surfaces, Fuchsian groups and quasiconformal deformation theory. In this paper, we provide a simple and short argument to the above realisation that also works for any countable group.
L105: ### Theorem 2
L106: 
L107: Let X be a surface and fix a topologically tame action \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\), where G is a countable (finite or infinite) group. Then there is a dessin \({\mathcal D}=(X,{\mathcal G})\) with \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) isomorphic to G and induced by the topological action of \(\theta (G)\).
L108: Let G be any countable group and let X be any surface of infinity type such that all of its ends are non-planar and its ends space is self-similar (see [【37†2】] for details). An example of such type of surfaces is, for instance, the Loch Ness monster (the unique, up to orientation-preserving homeomorphisms, infinite genus surface with exactly one end). In [【37†2】], Aougab-Patel-Vlamis proved that one can find a Riemann surface structure S on X such that \(\mathrm{Aut}(S)\) is isomorphic to G.
L109: So, the above theorem asserts the following existence fact (as already stated before).
L110: ### Corollary 1
L111: 
L112: Let X be a surface of infinite type, where all of its ends are non-planar and its ends space is self-similar. If G is a countable group, then there is a dessin \({\mathcal D}=(X,{\mathcal G})\) such that \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})\) isomorphic to G. In fact, such a dessin can be given in the Loch Ness monster.

L114: ## 2 Preliminaries
L115: ### 2.1 Locally finite branched coverings
L116: 
L117: A surjective continuous map \(Q:X \rightarrow Y\), where X and Y are surfaces, is called a locally finite branched cover if:
L118: 
L119:   1. (1)
L120: 
L121: the locus of branched values \(B_{Q} \subset Y\) of Q (it might be empty) is a discrete set;
L122: 
L123:   2. (2)
L124: 
L125: \(Q:X \smallsetminus Q^{-1}(B_{Q}) \rightarrow Y \smallsetminus B_{Q}\) is a covering map; and
L126: 
L127:   3. (3)
L128: each point \(q \in B_{Q}\) has an open connected neighbourhood U such that \(Q^{-1}(U)\) consists of a collection \(\{V_{j}\}_{j\in I}\) of pairwise disjoint connected open sets such that each of the restrictions \(Q|_{V_j}:V_{j} \rightarrow U\) is a finite degree branched cover (i.e., it is topologically equivalent to a branched cover of the form \(z \in {\mathbb D} \mapsto z^{d_{j}} \in {\mathbb D}\), where \({\mathbb D}\) denotes the unit disc).
L129: If X is a compact surface, then a branched covering is always locally finite. But, in the case that X is non-compact, a branched covering might not be locally finite.
L130: ### 2.2 Topologically tame actions
L131: 
L132: Let G be a group, X be a surface and \(\theta :G \rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X)\) be an injective homomorphism. We say that the action of \(\theta (G)\) is tame on X if there is a Galois locally finite branched cover \(Q:X \rightarrow Y\) with deck group \(\theta (G)\) (in particular, G is countable).
L133: ### 2.3 Belyi pairs and dessins
L134: Let \(S^{2}\) be the standard 2-dimensional sphere and fix three different points \(p_{0}, p_{1}, p_{\infty } \in S^{2}\).
L135: A dessin \({\mathcal D}=(X,{\mathcal G})\) defines a (unique up to isotopy) locally finite branched cover \(Q:X \rightarrow S^{2}\) with \(B_{Q} \subseteq \{p_{0},p_{1},p_{\infty }\}\), where \(Q^{-1}(p_{0})\) (respectively, \(Q^{-1}(p_{1})\)) are the black (respectively, white) vertices of \({\mathcal G}\) and there is an arc \(\delta =[p_{0},p_{1}] \subset S^{2} \smallsetminus \{p_{\infty }\}\), such that that \(Q^{-1}(\delta )={\mathcal G}\).
L136: Moreover, \(\mathrm{Aut}({\mathcal D})=\mathrm{Aut}(X,Q)=\{ \phi \in \mathrm{Hom}^{+}(X): Q \circ \phi =Q\}\). Note that, for X either of genus \(g \ge 1\) or of infinite type, then \(\#B_{Q}=3\). We say that the pair (X, Q), as above, is a Belyi pair. Conversely, given a Belyi pair (X, Q), where \(Q:X \rightarrow S^{2}\) is a locally finite branched cover with \(B_{Q} \subseteq \{p_{0},p_{1},p_{\infty }\}\), then it induces a dessin \({\mathcal D}\) as above.
L137: ### Remark 1
L138: Let (X, Q) be a Belyi pair.
L139: If \(\varphi :S^{2} \rightarrow \widehat{\mathbb C}\) is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism, where \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) denotes the Riemann sphere, with \(\varphi (B_{Q})\subseteq \{\infty ,0,1\}\), then we may pull-back the Riemann surface structure of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), under \(\varphi \circ Q\), in order to provide a Riemann surface structure S on X such that \(\varphi \circ Q:S \rightarrow \widehat{\mathbb C}\) is a non-constant meromorphic map with branch value set contained inside \(\{\infty ,0,1\}\).
